utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're on page 5 of the witness's summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you get there, just to deal with the arrangements for today and tomorrow may be convenient. We are in the middle of this witness. We think it right to say that, having considered the evidence and considered too the time constraints, that they should be applied to the Prosecution too and that you should finish with this witness today. So would you tailor your examination-in-chief to do so, and we shall say that cross-examination will follow, if necessary, tomorrow. If we can start earlier, so much the better. And we shall expect it to be, and in fact it must be, finished tomorrow. We'll give four and a half hours, which should be ample.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That leaves out the Rule 92 bis argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might that conveniently be taken next week in these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. When would be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's something I'm going to want to say about the order of witnesses right at the end of today, and probably in what's called private session because it may touch on a protected witness, but subject to that, Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient to deal with the timing of that argument when we hear about the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've heard, Mr. Kadriu, about the time constraints, and therefore, even more than yesterday, if you'll listen to my questions and, where possible, deal with them by yes/no answers, I would be grateful. We touched on the September 1998 offensive in the Cicavica Mountain. In that area, was there the presence of Serb forces, to your knowledge, in September 1998? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were villagers suffering, and, in a sentence, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They suffered because they were surrounded on all sides, and for the first time they were not allowed to leave their villages. But they were being subjected to an unprecedented terror and violence. There were killings, people injured, there were arrests of many people. About 30 people were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And very quickly, did you yourself receive information of a man in Pasome, a man of about 55 years of age?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 22nd of September, there were attacks on the village of Sllakofc and Pasome. On that occasion, a 55-year-old was killed and another one was injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were killed from the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see - just yes or no - villagers from Novolan who came to see you on the 22nd of September?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the village of Novolan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. May Exhibit 18 please be prepared for showing to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you become aware of forces in your area generally?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to explain to you. It was the morning of the 22nd of September when we realised that we were surrounded on all sides. We were informed by some villagers of Novolan village who are nearby. They had abandoned their houses when police intervened and came towards our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Novolan, by the way, Your Honours, can be found immediately north-east of Brusnik on map 4/10. I don't desire to see it on the overhead projector for reasons of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself see those forces? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if so, may the witness have Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Including the police and military forces later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will the witness please look at on the ELMO, on the overhead projector, Exhibit 18. Which, if any, uniforms here match what you saw on that occasion, the 22nd of September?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's number 6. Later, I saw people in number 9 uniform, and then there were some police or soldiers who were wearing kerchiefs on their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When did the Serbian forces withdraw from the area of your village Novolan and so on?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our village, they withdrew on the 24th, whereas from the other surrounding villages on the 25th, because there were two circles of encirclement, as it were, in the villages who were along the road which leads to Obilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you - just yes or no - tour neighbouring villages to discover the extent of damage caused?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from memory -- from memory, no doubt having reminded yourself from other records, can you tell us anything about the percentage or number of houses damaged in Oshlan?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Oshlan, there were about more than 70 per cent of the houses were burnt, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that's north-west of Brusnik. In Balinca?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Balinca, it was approximately a similar situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's also to the north-west. In Dubofc?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Dubofc, it was more than 80 per cent of the houses which were burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Dubofc south-west or is that not the same place?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dubofc is located -- let me say west of Vushtrri and my village. That's west.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made further inquiries last night. The Pristina information office that publishes the map I'm hoping to provide you has run out of them. We're making inquiries of the publishers themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okrashtica?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Okrashtica, there were fewer, comparatively fewer houses which were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's to the west of Vushtrri. And then in Pantina, which is just above --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pantina was most affected by the burning. More than 90 per cent of the houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Pantina is north of Okrashtica. And then --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: North-west of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Zhilivode?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zhilivode, too, 80 per cent of the houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't immediately located Zhilivode. Where is that in relation to your village?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This village is located south-west of Vushtrri and my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make inquiries in relation to the neighbouring municipalities; Mitrovica, Skenderaj, Gllogofc?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These municipalities, too, were surrounded from the 22nd to the 25th of September. They were surrounded like in a quarantine. And it was an iron encirclement in two layers. The second was the army. The second layer was the army with all the armoured vehicles and weapons. If you allow me to explain. On this occasion, there were killings in the mountain region of Cicavica and people were mutilated. It was the 22nd of September, 1998. Between the 22nd and the 24th, the people were displaced and had settled in Cicavica. That was before the police intervened, before the police raided their houses. And they left their houses to settle in the mountainous area Cicavica where they found many residents of the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, Mr. Kadriu, if you wouldn't mind, please, to deal with the following in summary simply for want of time. Galice is on the Skenderaj map, and it is itself north-east of Skenderaj, about halfway between there and the edge of the map. Did you find 14 men or 14 males there?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cicavica, after people had left from the Galice into Cicavica, 13 people had died and a woman was killed not far from the site where the 13 were killed. So it was 14 altogether from the village of Galice who were killed and massacred. It was a big tragedy for the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw the bodies, were they naked, piled on top of one another? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the information from a young man who said that in the village of Cicavica was terrible because the massacred bodies were placed one on top of the other. And we went there to see for ourselves. It was really terrible. There were young people who were mutilated. They had stuck their eyes out, and they had cut off parts of their bodies, and they were placed one on top of the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were six or seven there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see four men, or the bodies of four men in the mountain area Cicavica itself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was less than a kilometre away. There were four bodies. We investigated this with other people too. They were there. And from the horror they saw, because the crime was -- was committed with knives. There was -- they had slit their throats. They had been hit on their heads with a hammer and their brains were scattered around. And we have photographed this, and all the material is with the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Oshlan, which is back on the Vucitrn municipality map, just south of Vushtrri, across the -- I beg your pardon. It's west of Vushtrri and towards the left-hand side of the map. In Oshlan, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also in the village of Oshlan -- I went to Oshlan a bit later, though, because it was very difficult to move around because everywhere there were bodies. I went there in the evening. I didn't see the bodies because they were being prepared for burial, and there were women among those who were executed by the Serb forces, and they were buried that very night. At the same time when the burial of the bodies in Galice took place, I forgot to say that in the Cicavica mountain, those people who were executed in Galice, two or three of them were pupils, were students in our school. And for this we have documents to prove --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to move you so fast and in an apparently unsympathetic way, but it's just a matter of time. So in Oshlan, how many -- you may have told us. How many bodies did you see there or how many bodies were you told about there?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 15 bodies. The bodies of Oshlan, I couldn't see them for myself because they were prepared for burial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about that. Just yes or no: Did you speak to an elderly woman and her son? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they give you an account - yes or no - of the people who had committed the offences there? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they describe them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they were going up the mountain, the wife of the late person explained to us that they were surrounded on all sides, and they were approached by people who were wearing kerchiefs on their faces, and a policeman, as they say. She sometimes said "policemen," sometimes said "soldiers," but she's not educated. She begged them not to kill her husband because, before, they had killed the mother of her husband, and she wanted her husband to be safe. And as she was begging them not to kill him, they shot him dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she say --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And she was explaining all that to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she describe the uniform the policeman or soldier was wearing, and its colour?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was saying that they were mixed. Some were wearing kerchiefs on their faces, some were wearing blue uniforms, but there were also green uniforms and camouflage uniforms because very often --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- police was wearing anti-bullet -- bulletproof vests in these colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We move on briefly. In Zhilivode, did you see one body of a man? If so, his age approximately?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a very old man, between 70 and 90 years old. It was the body of a 70- to 90-year-old man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had his body been mutilated?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: His body did not have any limbs and it was difficult to bury him. He --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I need to know. In Bivolak -- I haven't located Bivolak yet, but don't worry about it. We'll find it if necessary. What did you see in Bivolak?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bivolak, in addition to a young man who was shot by guns, firearms, there was an adolescent girl. She was in her teens. She was shot. A shell had hit the trailer and she died as they were fleeing the village. Vitore Klinaku is her name, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the body of an old man there or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Bivolak and Zhilivode, there were killings. Some of them were discovered later. One of those killed was buried later, because the people tried to preserve the bodies so that they could identify them. Because some of them were so badly mutilated and transformed that they could hardly be identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to summarise the balance, coming back to it only if we have time at the end of the morning. Did you discover evidence of killings in Beciq, Balinca, Smrekovnica, and indeed in other places? Just yes to that if it's true.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of the body in Beciq, who I did not manage to see for myself, but I have it in my documents, and the victim there was a 60-year-old woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on now to Reznik. On the 25th of September of 1998, were you informed about the displaced persons in Reznik?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 25th of September, yes.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by two or three people who were coming from there, and they told me that an unprecedented number of people had managed to leave Cicavica, because many killings had happened there and they didn't dare stay there. They came to settle in Reznik. I tried to go there, but it was difficult to move around. It was difficult to reach the area because I had to go through several villages which were inhabited by Serbs, and the Serb police was still there, and I didn't succeed in going there. I was told that there was more than 50.000 people. They were hungry, they were frightened, wounded. And I phoned on my mobile to the Council of Human Rights that there a considerable number of people was being surrounded, so do what you can, because we are on the verge of a catastrophe. And the male civilians were separated from women and they were executed later. Later I informed the American office with the same mobile, because I thought that the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms did not have the authority or the strength or the power to do anything for those people, and later I was told that some bodies which had some influence had intervened to save these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will recall that Reznik is due south of Vushtrri, immediately across the railway lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the bodies that you were told --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reznik, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bodies you were told had visited the village included, did they, somebody comparatively well-known?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later, the Council of Human Rights of Freedoms told me not to worry about the fate of those people because in Pristina, Sadak Ogata happened to be there at the time, and she was the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. And on that occasion she had intervened, and with her arrival, the Serb leadership and the Serb army and police began to withdraw their forces and to put several buses from the Kosova Trans company to distribute the people from the area, to spread them around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did you understand had orders been given that this should be done?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was a secure situation because the then chairman of the municipality, who, as of the 16th of June, 1998, was appointed the chairman of the staff for military police, civilian, and humanitarian affairs, Slobodan Doknic, to do what he could to release these people and to send them home. Doknic himself had a gun, as far as I remember, there once, and he had ordered the tanks to withdraw from the road which is near the railway, and then military and police forces too withdrew, so the people could go where they could to find accommodation, to various homes in Vushtrri, Pristina, and elsewhere, because they could not return home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to touch on the role of Mr. Doknic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, through this witness we can deal directly with the structure of municipality crisis staffs that we would otherwise be dealing with by an expert, which is why I will focus -- we may deal with it by an expert or other witness in due course, but this witness may deal with these matters directly. May the witness now please have the next exhibit, which we've called SK3, in its original form and with the translation available. Can we place the original on the overhead projector. Can we place the original on the overhead projector, please, briefly, so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's in Cyrillic. We can see it has a list of names. We'll look at the translation in a second, but before we move from that: Is the signature one that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is signed by Slobodan Doknic. I know this signature, because the person who has signed this was a professor of mine when I was a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we then have the English version on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document bears a date, the 17th of June, 1998. It lists the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. members of the Vucitrn Municipality Crisis Staff and 11 names. Are those names all Serbs or are there any Kosovar Albanians listed there?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't any Albanians listed here. No, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move on to the arrival of the OSCE, KVM. Was that mission deployed between October 1998 and February 1999, and in your area, were things relatively quiet for some or most of that period?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation was not completely calm. It was relatively calm, with conflicts occurring now and then. The chairman of the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms, I asked this monitoring mission to open an office in Vushtrri too, because until then, the office was only in Mitrovica. Because of the violence, we asked them to be placed under their monitoring and control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In February 1999, was there shelling again in the Cicavica Mountains?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. At the end of February 1999, there was shelling of Cicavica, and the local Serbs of the villages thereby, together with police forces, were organised and patrolling the streets which were leading to our villages, to Albanian villages, that is. That was the same also in Novolan, Troje ose village, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for villagers who were compelled to move, did they move to Vushtrri, and was this the first, second, or third time that many of them had been compelled to move?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know for sure. It probably was the third time for even my own family members to leave their home. In this case too, they were forcibly evicted from their house by the police, who entered to every house and forced the people to leave. The same happened with my family in March. They settled in Vushtrri, all of them, while once the people left, the houses were set fire to. We could see from Vushtrri our homes on fire and in flames. The smoke and the smell came up to Vushtrri town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only of our village, but also of the other surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Serb forces achieve control of the area, if they ever did?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was by middle of March, I think, when the military forces, with tanks, penetrated in some parts west of Vushtrri. In Vulan [phoen] they settled earlier, Okrashtica, then they arrived in a village near Cicavica hills. So they had penetrated, as I said, in several remote villages inhabited mainly by Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the OSCE leave Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE did a great job to mediate and to prevent conflicts arising between the Serb army and people who were fleeing their homes, as well as the KLA. That was settled in Cicavica. From what I remember, it was 19th of March when the OSCE left Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to their office and their houses?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is interesting to know that, once they left, on the next day, the first house that was set fire to in Vushtrri was the house which used to be the offices of the OSCE, and then the houses where its official representatives lived also was burned. Then the largest part of the town began to be torched every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the 24th and -- I beg your pardon. Between the 22nd and the 24th of March, did you receive reports of people being injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were injured people and people who got killed every day. I think it was the 22nd of March. I was in town, together with my family. We were staying with my uncle. I heard that a colleague of ours, a professor - his name is Skender Bllaca - he was executed in the most mysterious way near the road and his body was thrown in a ditch. I may inform you that Skender was being wanted by the police even earlier, who kept demanding money from him. They asked him to give them about 20.000 Deutschmark. I don't know what that was. He had managed so far to escape the police, but on the 21st of March, a jeep of green colour had taken him away and had executed him. The next day I saw his body with Miran Halili [phoen] and took him to his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from that one person, just by number, how many other deaths in like or similar circumstances were reported?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact number, but I know that another man was killed in Vulan [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can't give an exact number I'm going to move on. Or even an estimate. Can you give an estimate of how many people were killed in that two-day period or three-day period?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 22nd of September, I wrote a report for the OSCE, and you perhaps can find that report in their documents. The number of killed was about 70. Some were injured, some were arrested. As of 22nd of September, they were in Mitrovica prison. Some were sent to Serbia. The number of the arrested persons might be about 30. Most of them were released from gaol. Some of them, maybe five or six, were taken to Serb prisons where they served their sentence until late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You've given a figure, but I want you to give it again. Just the figure. How many of those were killed, on your recollection? If you don't have a recollection, don't guess.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of 22nd of September up to now that we are talking, there were about 70 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not 22nd of September. We're concerned, and it may be my mistake, I'm concerned simply in the period 22nd to the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The summary is not very clear on this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What number were reported killed, if you can help, and don't guess if you can't.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. You mean the 22nd until the 24th of March. I can't give you an exact number. People were killed, but the relevant document on that incident got burned, so I don't have the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did NATO bombing begin on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the evening of 24th of March when NATO bombing began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Albanian people happy or sad about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanian people were very happy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were under --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... time. A few days later, did you become aware of where the Serbs were gathering in Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was on the second day, that is, on the 25th. In the afternoon hours I was at my uncle's, as I said, staying with my family. This apartment is located near the school, and from the window we saw when the police forces, together with civilians, people, some of whom you might know, arrived there. They were Serb citizens of Vushtrri. Since they didn't have a key to the door, they broke it down with an axe. It was a strong iron door with some glass windows, parts. And I think they form the headquarters of that neighbourhood there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the following days, were houses in Vushtrri subject to looting and burning and damage of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Houses were burnt constantly. Burning went on up until very late at night. It started in the northern part of Vushtrri. Then it went on in the eastern part. And this operation continued in the centre. It was difficult for people to move from their homes because they had to pass through many police roadblocks who checked all the ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in Vushtrri from the seventh century?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three mosques, but one of them dated back to the seventeenth -- sorry, to the, yes, seventeenth century. It was situated in the centre of Vushtrri. There was also an oriental complex of homes, because Vushtrri, per se, is a very old city. And it started to burn. It was the 28th of March when the mosque started to burn, along with the complex around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Serbs calling anything or saying anything that might have been provocative?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house I was staying -- I had already abandoned the previous apartment at my uncle's because it was surrounded by police forces. I can tell you that on that afternoon, close to where we were staying where a house was burnt which used to be the house of OSCE member staff, we left, went, took to the hills. Together with us there were many other citizens. And we stayed at another relative of ours. On the 28th, looting and raiding and large-scale burning began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you realise the time problems we have. You haven't answered my question. I know it's difficult. It would help me ration the time and use it to the maximum -- make best use of it. Just yes or no: Did you hear Serbs calling anything out in the course of these operations that you've described? If so, what sort of things were they calling out?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When -- since we were not very far from the centre -- actually, we were close. They were shouting, "Allah, Allah," all the time that the mosque was burning. We couldn't see them, but the fire, I mean, could be seen. The flames could be seen from our home, and we were scared that it, too, might be burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 29th of March, did you learn of bodies lying near the old bridge in the middle of Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brother and an aunt of our relatives who had come from another part of the town told us that in the vicinity of the old bridge, the stone bridge, there were two or three executed bodies that had been lying there for two days, even though the police were close by, checking and controlling the road leading out to other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with things chronologically, Your Honour, I'm going to ask the witness, with the Court's indulgence, to look at the next exhibit, indicated as SK4 in the summary. It is a handwritten book for which there is no translation, but the only thing I desire to have translated, if the witness can read it out from the original and we can follow, is the heading of what is a list of names. And if that could be made available to him. And to save time, if that could go straight onto the ELMO. These, then, for everybody else. Thank you. I will obtain a translation, if the document is admitted into evidence, of the title page, of the title, and have it made available as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, can you just move the book so we can see the title? Thank you very much. Can you read what is at the top of that page, please. Just the title.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first line reads: "The list of tasks" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just read it out, if you can.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: "List of tasks and commitment to ensure the general protection of the population in Vushtrri."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not so very well familiar with Serbian myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't follow that. What is the heading at the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what the witness has read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there is a heading right at the top. I thought he was reading the second row. I might have been mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour may be right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very top word. What's the top word, please?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heading says "List." The "List." Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is -- then we see a list of names with dates starting on the 23rd of -- 25th of March and spanning periods until April of 1999. We have those lists. We have those names before us. Where did this document come from, please?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found this document after the war in an office of the municipality where the popular defence staff was staying during the war, in room number 8 of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the names here, are they names of Serbs or are there names of Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, they are Serbs. And among these names, I know someone who is from Novolan village, a village nearby my town. I know the names of one or two Serbs whom I know really existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that document have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we then look at Exhibit SK5, as it's described, for which there is a draft translation. I beg your pardon; the final translation is available. Your Honour, this document and a great number of other documents have associated with them declarations of authenticity as to where they have been found, made by an investigator and indeed the senior investigator at the time in charge of matters in Kosovo. I don't wish to burden the Registry with paper that it may not require. If there's any challenge to the authenticity or provenance of these documents, then I can make these documents available as they're produced. Alternatively, I can keep them back until it becomes an issue, which is what I would prefer to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this document at which you're looking --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the original can go on the overhead projector so that we can just see it once. And then if the original can go to the witness with the English draft -- with the English final translation onto the ELMO, onto the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- titled "The Republic of Serbia, Ministry of Interior, Secretariat of the Interior for Kosovska Mitrovica," and then coming down, being the police station at Vucitrn on the 11th of January, 1999, listing something called "RPO," or, "OUP, members who were issued with automatic and semi-automatic rifles"? And then there are a number of names with rifle numbers and the bullets they were provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can that have an Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then next in the small collection of exhibits produced at this stage, may the witness have the document identified in the summary as SK6, a report of the 29th of March. Original, please, straight onto the overhead projector. Straight onto the overhead projector original. And translations. Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you one more question about the last exhibit, but I'll come to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The original then is on the overhead projector. May that now be substituted by the English translation and may the witness have the original in front of him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document signed by the same Slobodan Doknic?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know his signature very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Being a decision apparently of the Vucitrn municipality Crisis Staff, recording at a meeting held on the 29th of March, pursuant to an Article 2 of the decision on education and so on, that an order issuing authority is appointed for execution of Crisis Staff under war circumstances of the Vucitrn municipality, and it says the transfer account number. And it says "Slobodan Doknic, the President of the Crisis Staff under war circumstances." Yes?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it fit with your understanding of the position he was then holding as President of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to make an explanation, if possible. As of 1998, according to the previous documents, from the 16th of June, all the regular body which was the Municipal Assembly in Vushtrri, after the establishment of the Crisis Staff, this Assembly was overruled by this body. The Crisis Staff assumed all the powers then. It was called the Political, the Military, and Civilian Staff. Sometimes it was called the Staff for Military Affairs, sometimes the Crisis Staff. That is, in all the documents you will see it named by civilian names. The fact is that there were -- there was no more Assembly of the municipality after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 1st or 2nd of April or thereabouts, what happened to the occupants, inhabitants of Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, the population started to leave the town, mainly going east of Vushtrri. On the 2nd of April, from the centre of the city, police started to go house -- to every house and tell the inhabitants to leave. Therefore, like all the other inhabitants, we too decided to leave. We went to the road where we were told to go. Everybody knew that we were supposed to get together at the cemetery. And then we didn't know what would happen afterwards. Once we arrived at the cemetery, there was a large group of people there. It seemed to us that the whole city had turned out there. Three buses came belonging to Hajra Tours, which the -- the drivers of which said that we were supposed to go to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see Exhibit 18, please, the uniforms montage again. Did I get an exhibit number for SK6? Sorry. May I have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At some stage, Mr. Nice, we'll have to know what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. In a way, I think the witness has dealt with it by his summary of his understanding of the position of Doknic at that time, and there will be some other documents dealing with and some other evidence dealing with what the Crisis Staff was engaged in doing at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The English translation doesn't make much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is the final translation, though. It's what we've got. And, of course, he's not himself a person who has this as his first language. So, yes, I entirely agree. We will need some further assistance with it. May the witness look at Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the movement of people to the cemetery, what, if any, uniforms did you see, please?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed in uniforms I see in photo number 6, but they didn't have helmets there. I recognised him accompanied by two people. I saw Dragan Petrovic, who was deputy commander of the police chief of Vushtrri. Dragan Petrovic led this expedition. I saw him with my own eyes. I didn't see carefully his escorts, because I was afraid they might detect me; therefore, I left in haste and mixed up with a crowd of people who were leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dragan Petrovic was dressed how? You're saying he was dressed as in uniform number 6, without the helmet?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dressed in camouflage uniform, but he did not have the bulletproof vest underneath. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other uniforms from that montage that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not see the uniforms because I had to leave, out of fear that he knew about my activity in the context of human rights and freedoms protection. So I left and mixed up with people and didn't wait for him to come closer, fearing that he might arrest me or do something else to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What attitude did you take to this forced movement of people from the area? What, if anything, did you try and persuade the people to do?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were really scared. They moved by their own cars. Someone walked. They all went to the cemetery, as I said, where the buses came. I felt deep pain. I thought that this was the last time we were seeing Kosova and would not return there any more. So I talked to someone: Why should we leave Kosova? Let's go to some other place. And if they are going to execute, let them execute all of us. Some people tried to respond and think about what I said, and then later I realised that I was not right. They were right, because if we went to the cemetery, many people would have been executed. So we got on buses. Some went by their cars, some by tractors, some on foot. Despite the rain, they walked towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you land up? In which village?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy continued along the main road and I took shelter in one house on the outskirts of the city, and I walked to the other side of the region, which is called Shale e Bajgores, because I didn't want to go to Macedonia and leave Kosova altogether. I felt pain to do that. So my family came back to Vushtrri and stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And in Vushtrri itself or in a village outside Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I settled in a village outside Vushtrri. At the beginning I went to Studime e Eperme, and the second night I spent between the village of Sllakofc -- at a friend of mine who is the local president of the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms, and there I stayed for a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is all going from Vushtrri, on map 4/10, north-east. One can see the road leading up there, and that becomes of some significance in a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many refugees, approximately, were there in that area, that road leading up through Studime towards Cecile and Sllakofc?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is of interest to stress that the convoy which was going towards Macedonia, they managed to leave the convoy and settle in the villages along the main road between Mitrovica and Pristina, and they settled in the mountainous areas there. There were three areas where the people had amassed. There were people from Podujeva, Vushtrri, and Mitrovica. They had settled in this mountainous area because it was more relaxed and safer there. It was controlled by the Kosovo Liberation Army. And we thought that we could be safer, a great safety there. But there was no food. Food was not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many refugees, roughly, in the area where you were?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were residents from more than three communes. More than 30.000. And that was the region stretching from the vicinity of Pristina. And all the houses there were full of people, but there were people who were staying the nights in trailers, in a very difficult situation, without water, without food. And I was thinking about this, because if I had a mobile, I was going to phone human rights organisations to tell them what hell it was in that area, and we -- the people lacked the minimum of conditions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we have map 4/10 available for the witness in a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, at the end of April, become aware of shelling in the area of Popovo?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that case, yes. We were taking a walk with a friend of mine, and as we were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Kadriu, I know it's difficult for you because these are important matters of your own history. We've gone through an hour and ten minutes and we've got through four pages, and we're only just going to be able to finish the evidence by the end of the morning at this speed. We're going to have to go faster and you're going to have to reduce the detailed account. If you'd like to have a look at the map, please. It's coming your way. Map 10 of Exhibit 4. And if we focus immediately on the area north-east of Vushtrri, if you'd like to point out the Studime area where you were and others of the 30.000 were.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's there. Now, if you look at that road, there's a road which has a sort of bend in it between Vushtrri and then going up to Studime. Were there people living in that area there - just yes or no - refugees?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Studime e Poshtme village, there were no people. They were evacuated and had settled in the mountainous area. It's very close to the city. They had left much earlier. But in the Studime e Eperme village, there were people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look still at the map, you've spoken of the shelling in Popovo or whatever it was. We'll hear about that in a minute. That is to be seen a little to the north and to the east, towards the edge of the map. Just point that out.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There. Thank you very much. Was it shelling or bombing or what that you heard of, and if so, by whose forces?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard bombing. We didn't know what was going on. That night, we were informed that there were killed people, people who were killed. And we went to Popova, together with my friend, and there we saw two Mig aircraft which had flown over the valleys and dropped bombs, thinking that there was the headquarters of the Kosovo Liberation Army. Several people were killed on that occasion, and among those killed there were girls, as well as males, and we attended the funeral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we come, in order that we can deal with things chronologically, to a couple of other documents. Can you look, please, at SK7, to see what was happening elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Original immediately to the ELMO and distribution of copies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, then, again over Doknic's signature, 17th of April, Crisis Staff decision, just as an example, that Milislav Kostic, the owner of an enterprise, would be mobilised and the lorry would be placed at the disposal of the Crisis Staff. Now, is Kostic, incidentally, a Serb name?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, do you remember we looked earlier at a document showing the distribution of rifles and ammunition? Were the names on that list - we don't have to look at it again - Serb, or Serb and Kosovar Albanian, or a mixture, or what, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Serb names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was part of the list. And he is from the village of Prelluzhe, of the Vushtrri municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document we'll look at shortly, SK8.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry. I keep forgetting that. And this one, original straight to the overhead projector, if you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just a clarification in the document just admitted. The lorry that would be placed at the disposal of the Crisis Staff is a lorry belonging to the enterprise Cobanka?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document at which we are now looking is the 21st of April, 1999, and this doesn't come from Doknic. It's from someone else. But it says as a consequence of war actions in the territory of your municipality, there are abandoned cattle and nobody to look after them. So to prevent the cattle from straying, perishing, and since there are citizens interested in grazing and breeding cows in the area of Leposavic municipality, we would appreciate if you would approve of providing 200 head of dairy cows from your area, would be allotted to citizens for grazing and breeding. And then it's signed by President Dragan Jablanovic for the Leposavic Crisis Serb area, and that's going to the crisis headquarters in Vushtrri. Is this from one crisis headquarters to another, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was issued by the same Crisis Staff, but I must explain that Leposaviq is a town which is north of Kosova and largely inhabited by Serbs. And the Albanian property, which were the properties which were looted from the Albanians, were sent -- stuff looted was sent to Leposaviq for the needs of the citizens there or for the needs of the army there. There was large-scale crime in this respect. This is just a document, but at that time there were many cases when the property of the Albanians was used for the needs of the Serbian army and police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Move on in the narrative. In May of -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 38. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the end of May of 1999, had the position changed in that the KLA were giving different advice as to what people should be doing?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the night of the 1st of May when we were informed that the Serbian forces were advancing on all fronts, and some members of the army, of the KLA, said that because of the lack of ammunition and weapons, they were no longer in a position to cope with the offensive. So they advised: Do what you can to go to safer places, because if you stayed there in that area, that would be dangerous. So many people decided to go towards Vushtrri and then to Macedonia. So the offensive progressed and approached the area surrounding the villages of Sllakofc, and the artillery moving. On the 2nd of May, a big convoy of people began to be created, moving towards Vushtrri. Even before, people were trying and then managed to get into Vushtrri, and they had paid their way out of the dangerous area, and that was on the way which passes via Studime. A woman from the village of Kolle had been to get some food in Vushtrri, and as she was coming back, where the river passes, the Serbian forces which were deployed in the hills nearby, they shot and killed her. Three other people were also killed in similar circumstances. But the situation was very difficult from the point of view of lack of food and water, and it was made worse from the intervention of the police and army, of the Serb police and army, and now the column was on its way towards Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this convoy is the subject of an amateur video; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me know if the witness was on it. It's not clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on this convoy yourself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the rest of the population -- and myself and my friend were the last to join this column. There was an unprecedented number of people, and the column was kind of stood put, was staying in place, because the road was overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All we want to know is whether you were on it. That's the only point for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's the subject of a video; correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have a videotape which is about the massacre that took place on the night of the 2nd of May, when within one hour, starting from 9.00 in the evening, a massacre was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has there also been a report prepared with photographs and an extensive map of this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have prepared a technical report describing the route of the convoy before the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have managed, although this document only arrived recently, we have managed to have it copied and to have it associated with a legend that provides a translation. If I can produce that now before any break, then I'd perhaps ask the Chamber, if it has time in the break, simply to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could find out who the "we" was who prepared it that the witness referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While these are offered for distribution --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was prepared by a group of experts, lawyers. From the technical point of view, there was another person who, before he was sacked from his job, he worked for the Kosovo police. He did not have good equipment, but he was the one who managed to produce this technically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a look on this document. It has in the front part of it on yellow paper - white paper in the photocopy - a long map showing the route of the convoy. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's a little part that's --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that lifts up from that in the middle of it, showing where bodies were buried and later exhumed, I think, by the ICTY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. To this day, in this site, there are the graveyards where the exhumation was carried out by the ICTY investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps it should be made clear whether any of this work is this witness's work or the work of someone else. It's certainly not clear to me at the moment. I think the Trial Chamber should be satisfied as to the nature of the document that's now being presented for it and whether this witness can properly speak to it. There's been no notice that he's an expert witness or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. And it's untranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a legend, and if it hasn't been distributed, that's an oversight. Here comes the legend. But I'll get the witness to deal with his contribution to the document in any event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The things set out on this report, are these some or all of the things you saw yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are the things that are set out here or some or all of them things that you saw yourself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the report was compiled, were you involved in its compilation or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the supervisors. I was organising the work that was being done. It was the expert personnel who was carrying out the actual reporting, who was compiling the report, and the person who worked before 1990 for the Kosova police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it prepared for your organisation?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not know that this court was going to be organised. We were thinking about processes which would start in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, what I would like to do, apart from have the document exhibited and available for inspection over the next break, is just to ensure that the Chamber understands where the route shown on the pull-out plan is reflected on the map itself. I think that would be helpful. So if the witness could now have Exhibit 4/10, the map again, on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at the overhead projector, please, Mr. Kadriu, and tell us where the road shown on the pull-out plan is shown on the map on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Studime e Eperme village. We passed via Studime, and we continued the route towards Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is as I -- it's the road with the bend in it that I drew to your attention earlier, starting at Studime and ending up in Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the map, we have the road from the Studime e Eperme and the other villages have not been included, and the population was coming from all the surrounding villages. But on the map here, we have the road from Studime to Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is on the front? Do we have that translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we haven't got that translated, that's an oversight. Perhaps the witness can read it out. It is in his language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the cover of the -- no, absolutely the cover. No. This bit here, Mr. Kadriu. Can you read that out in your own language? I will have it translated.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It writes: "The sketch with pictures on the case of Studime e Eperme and Studime e Ulet on the date of the -- dated May, 1999," it's the, "2nd of May, 1999, where people who have been Albanians who were leaving the area were executed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the title in printed script, or in print, rather, what does that read? Can you just read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It writes in both languages because at that time we did not have relevant documentation. It writes in Albanian: "The bundle of documents," and then it's in Serbo-Croat, which is the same material. These files were used for the needs of the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I would say, Mr. Nice, is that the map is a very graphic illustration of the length of the convoy, because I am unable to pull it out to its full length with one arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can understand that. I'm very grateful to those who managed to put this together at such short notice, but it seemed appropriate to have it in the identical form for the Court as it existed in the original. I don't know if that can be given an exhibit number, and if by its production before the break I will be able to make great savings of time about the convoy after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I know you've been making as good speed as possible. We understand that there is a problem as far as the accused is concerned in sitting late because of the visit by his wife only being available today. So the greater speed we could make, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall do my very best. Exhibit -- before we move on, Exhibit 36, the document the Chamber could not understand. If I said it was a final translation, I was wrong. It's a draft translation. And I'm grateful to the interpreters in the booth who unraveled the dilemma a little bit. The word "education" is a mistranslation. A similar word, but in fact it's "establishment." So Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that in the first line, the document should read: "At its meeting on the 29th of March, 1999, pursuant to Article 2 on establishment of the Municipal Council." That, I think, renders the document more intelligible. Your Honour, if we can return to the evidence of the witness. The video of which he speaks is one that I think the Chamber has already seen. The six-minute extract that has been carefully and helpfully compiled is one I will not play unless I find I have time before the end of the morning. The Chamber having now had the advantage of seeing the general form of preparation of the exhibit that's just been produced, I propose to go through the witness's account of incidents in the convoy in as short a period of time as I properly can, just getting him to deal with particular events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, forgive my compelling you to be brief but it's essential we do so. You've already explained to the Judges that you were certainly initially at the end of the convoy, and you've told us about there being up to 30.000 people in it. Did there come a time - and please use yes or no answers wherever you can - did there come a time --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the convoy appeared to stop, to come to a halt? I think that "yes," will do to that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column, convoy, was stopped at about 50 -- 17 hours. That is at 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a 17-year-old girl found to have died as a result of something?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Upper Studime, when we heard fire coming from all sides, this young girl was injured and died afterwards. She was injured in Upper Studime --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when we started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn of who was at the head of the column and what they were apparently doing?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw that the convoy was very slow in moving because of the very large number of people. Then we found out that the column was headed by three representatives who were waving a white cloth, and we were moving in the direction of Vushtrri so that the Serb forces who were stationed along and -- along the road and especially in a hill didn't fire at us. But they kept firing now and again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the front of the convoy? If so, who did you find to be leading it?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the head of the column was a 65-year-old man by the name of Brahim Muliqi; then Bajram -- Muharrem Shabani, former deputy of Kosovo parliament; and then Professor Bajram Mulaku. And we consulted them as to why the convoy was stopped, and they said that it was getting late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a white flag?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a white flag which they had put on a concrete hole -- pole so that the Serb forces could see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, at 9.00 p.m., hear sounds of forces, Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were settled there on the fields, some sitting on their tractors, at the end -- by the end of the convoy we heard some shouts. We thought they were police and soldiers' shouts. Then people's shouts, then the roar of the engines. Then we heard fire shots, gunshots, and people were getting killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb forces give any instructions to the convoy that you heard?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were hearing people being killed at the end of the convoy, we didn't know why, but later found out why. We saw that -- I mean, some Serb forces had entered the convoy. It was night. We couldn't be sure who was in the convoy: who was police, who was soldier, and so on. I heard them saying -- there were three people. I saw one of them as a silhouette. He was accompanied by two others. They said, "The convoy should come after us," and they were insulting us. And this is what we did. At the beginning, I didn't leave right away, but then we did follow them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of this period of time, did you hear anything being said over Serb radios?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had not made a long way before I heard some policeman or soldier. I'm not sure, because it was dark, very dark. He smelled of alcohol. I heard that he was talking on the radio. Before that, he killed someone ahead of us. It was about 20 metres before us. He placed a battery in front of people's faces -- he placed a torch in front of people's faces, and then we saw him kill one of the people in the convoy. He threw his body on the river bank. We were very scared and feared that he would recognise us and kill us too. Then after about 50 metres, we could hear very well the sound of the radio. He was asking someone, "How many until now?" That was what he said. This was heard not only by me but by others. And we heard him saying, "Sixty." I thought he was talking about people being killed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when the convoy was split in two, at a time when you were aware there were no Serbian escorts near you?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They escorted us for a time and then this guy stopped behind. The others were at the beginning of the convoy. For a moment we heard some shots. I think it came from some mortars [as interpreted]. I have done the military service. I think they were grenades. The first grenade fell in the river. I heard children cry. The cries were so horrible that I could never forget them, even when I was in gaol. Then we heard two other grenades fall, but I wasn't sure where they did fall or where they did come from, and then I saw the convoy stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the convoy start again in due course, and were you taken to the agricultural cooperative in Vushtrri itself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were walking, people were being shot. We heard the gunshots. We continued helping each other. We helped a mother who was carrying a child on her back. That mother knew nothing of her own family. We helped her until we went near the city. There we saw other forces coming towards us in cars, and we were afraid that they would recognise us and so left the lady alone. Together with Fadil, we followed with the others in the convoy. Once we arrived at the entrance to the city, we saw that all the doors of the houses that were empty now were ajar. Some were very scared and thought -- without knowing where we were going. And we wanted to leave the convoy, but the fact was that in those houses that we believed were empty were Serb troops who were ready. Once someone tried to leave the convoy, they fired at them. This was the case with two people who attempted to flee the convoy, which happened in the vicinity of Vushtrri before going to the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've come, as it were, to the end of the convoy, because you're in Vushtrri, in the cooperative. The Judges have the report that was prepared. Can you just help me with one detail so that we can understand it. In the map that is produced as part of the report, there's the pop-up or fold-out part that deals with the graveyard and has a legend attached to it starting at numbers 9, I think, roughly, dealing with the graveyard. In as short a period of time as you can, just a couple of sentences, can you explain the history of events that led to this graveyard? Where were the bodies killed that were buried there? When were they buried there?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The murders started at about 9.00 in the evening and continued even after midnight, while the convoy kept moving and people kept being shot. People were shot mainly in the road between Studime e Eperme and Poshtme, where we had decided to spend the night so that we could find out what happened next morning. While the executions were taking place, Studime e Eperme and other villages were being torched. We could see this very well because of the flame that shone in the sky that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the people who were killed come to be buried at that particular site that we know was subsequently exhumed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 109 people who got killed that night in a short period of time. One hundred and four or one hundred and three were buried in Studime e Eperme on the next day, after their bodies were collected by some people who were sheltered in the mountains, ordinary people, but also by the KLA, who returned one day later. Some of the soldiers of the KLA returned on the next day and helped the farmers bury the dead bodies executed on the night of the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can now pick up the story in the agriculture cooperative. When you were taken there, was anything said - just yes or no - about what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you told was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were entering the cooperative -- because the cooperative and the factory that there is there are divided by a road. While we were entering it, we saw a motorised convoy of Serbs. I think it was led by two tanks. Then the others were armoured cars and APCs. There were about 17 of them. When they were driving past us, they told us that, "We have orders to kill all of you, whereas your wives, your sisters, we have raped all of them up there," up there when the crime scene was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. May the witness be shown in due course Exhibit 17, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who appeared to you to be in charge or one of the officers in charge of people at the time?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody who was there - not only myself, those eyewitnesses who saw their relatives being killed - said that first the army passed, then they were followed by other groups of policemen whom they knew. They knew the police chief, Vucina Janicevic [phoen], Ljubisa Simic, Petrovic. When we arrived at the courtyard, I heard myself one policeman shouting in Serbian, saying, "Where is Petrovic?" The other answered, "He's coming." And then they herded us in the cooperative storehouses which are about 30 or 50 metres long. I am not sure about the size of these storehouses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move along to what happened inside, Exhibit 17, please. Can you look at this on the overhead projector and tell us which, if any, vehicles you are now able to recognise as vehicles that you saw on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was number 4. The tank might be like this one here, the two tanks that I saw. One was at the beginning. The two others were at the end of the convoy of armoured cars. There was a truck like this and like this one here, 8. But on both sides they had two rubber tyres. This type here, this APC --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 9.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was also used. Number 14 that I see here, from 1997, end of 1997 and 1998, they saw such kind of cars patrolling the streets, but not white like this, but of dark green, I think. SMB, dark SMB. They had dark glasses [as interpreted]. You could not see inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in what uniforms, if you were able to recognise the uniforms, were the men dressed who were controlling the convoy and its move to the agricultural cooperative?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night it was dark. Until after 10.00 it was really very dark. Then the moon started to shine. On the next day, in the courtyard of the cooperative, I saw camouflage blue uniforms that were usually worn by the police, as well as some other uniforms that the police used to wear in the past, only blue. On their shoulders, I remember very well they had some insignia which -- I think it was red and green and maybe white. Blue and white, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We must move on. On the 3rd of May -- I beg your pardon. You were detained overnight. Roughly how many civilians had arrived with your group?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My group -- I told you the convoy was separated in two parts. My group didn't have more than 1.000 persons. They pushed us. "Go to this warehouse."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kadriu --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But people arrived all night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
