utterances.text: It's a pity to abbreviate your account, but we have to. The people arriving, were some of them injured? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some injured and some killed who people had brought, their bodies, had brought in their trailers. People who had been executed in those very trailers, and they had kept them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb police who were controlling you offer any type of aid to those who were injured?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember very well this detail. Next morning, it was about 9.00, a mother whose child wanted water -- we were all thirsty. We were standing. People were crammed there, and the courtyard was full of people. I remember that lady trying to go to a fountain to get some water. The Serb forces who were deployed along the road and who looked at us --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, thank you very much. We get the point. No water was provided.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not -- allow me please to finish this detail, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let counsel decide what's important, please, Mr. Kadriu. He knows what's relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, the only reason we're abbreviating it is because there is a finite amount of time that we have. The 3rd of May, was there a separation of men from women?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 3rd of May at about 10.00, they came and ordered us to separate men from women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the women and children indeed go to an adjacent field and did they appear to be being registered?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They ordered us that people -- men from the age of 15 or 17 - I am not very sure - up to 17 -- 75 should stay on the -- on one side of the yard. The women and the children shall stay in the yard where we all were before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of this operation?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in charge of this operation was Dragan Petrovic. Vujanovic was not there that day. Draganovic led the expedition. And Dragan Mihajlovic from Maxhunaj village - he worked in the secret police service in Vushtrri - was there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of operations at this time, did something happen to a man called Ali Mernica?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were waiting for the trucks to transport us to the prison of Smrekovnica, there is a narrow street that separates the yard. Then we saw two policemen calling -- talking with family members of Ali Mernica. Then we saw him being taken away. Then they crossed the road and went to the extra factory yard. Then we saw --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. What was Ali Mernica well known for having done earlier in relation to education?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that at the time when we were dismissed from schools during 1991, he gave his three houses for -- put them at the disposal of Albanian teachers to use them for education purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was taken aside by the police. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the police stopped. The other accompanied him behind the factory where we couldn't see what was happening, but we heard the gunshots. Then we heard the policeman returning alone. The other part of the population were being registered on the other part of the road where the civilian population --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed Ali Mernica had been shot dead?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard that Ali Mernica was executed that day. And his body was exhumed by the ICTY. His corpse was found, because we didn't know where he was buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the -- were the documentation of men checked?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They checked all our documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to keep your documentation at this stage or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment until we were in the yard of the cooperative, they checked our documents and separated us. They took some of us who were drivers and they told them to stay aside, whereas we who were supposed to go to prison were told to stay aside. The operation went on simultaneously. The population was transported --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All you were asked was whether you were allowed to keep your documentation. Mr. Kadriu, could you just listen to the question and just give a fairly short answer. If there are relevant matters, counsel will mention them. Were you allowed to keep your documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At that place, yes. They returned our documents back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the same time, were Serb police telling you something about where you were to go or where people were to go?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell us anything. Many people went to police and offered them money, up to 2.000 Deutschmark, just to let them escape. I remember that other people on the other side of the street were shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause. Was anything said to people about where they were to go? Was anything said about Albania at this stage? Just yes or no, and if yes, what?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know where they were taking these people, but we saw them being escorted by police on both sides. We were sitting there with our hands tied behind our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just look at another document to see what's been recorded in the Crisis Staff at this time, SK9. The original straight to the overhead projector. This is a document dated the 3rd of May, recording a decision of the municipal Crisis Staff. We can now put the English version on the ELMO and hand the original to the witness. Thank you very much. The decision is by the same Slobodan Doknic, recording that the municipal Crisis Staff should establish a census-taking commission, the named individuals to take a census as soon as possible, and associated orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any census-taking at that stage by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were seeing the census being taken, that is, the registration of people, of civilians, and we knew those people who were registering --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were then, I think, taken to Smrekovnica prison.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Smrekovnica prison, were your documents checked, and if so, by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what type of person?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived there by trucks that were taken away from the Albanians. We were in the last truck. We were transported to Smrekovnica prison at 4.00. We arrived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived there, we saw Serb security people seated in some long tables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your documents checked? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were checked. We were all registered. Then they pushed us against the wall, some others, some other guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did the police treat you on arrival or when you were pushed against the wall?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very badly. Someone has hit his head or his forehead on the wall, if you were not careful, because they forced us to face the wall --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- after we were registered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were registered. Was that the ordinary police who were doing these things to you or was that the secret police?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The registration was done by the secret police. I recognised Janic there. Simic was from Vernica village, not far away from us. We used to work in the secret police. And some others I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now -- and you were taken to a cell. The dimensions of the cell and the number of people in it? And that's all I want from you on that.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were placed in a hall in the second floor, and in the cell where I was taken, it was 4 by 5 metres. We were not more than 17 or 18 people at the beginning, but then when other inmates came, we became 63 people shut in one -- in the same cell. Even the corridors were full of prisoners. People used to sleep in the toilet too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many days were you kept in a cell in those numbers?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 3rd of May up to the 23rd of May when we were released and deported to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness now see Exhibit SK10. Again, Your Honour, associated declarations by the investigator are available for this document if its provenance or accuracy is challenged in any way. All right. English version onto the overhead projector, original to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document from Vucitrn Department of the Interior, dated the 3rd of May, to the -- with the department heading that's -- an expansion of which is unknown, to the Secretariat of the Interior and to the heads of the Department of Police, the Criminal Investigation Department, as well as to the duty service shift leader for Kosovska Mitrovica. And does the document we all see is signed by someone called Ljubisa Simic, assert that on the 3rd of May, 1999, members of the police force engaged in breaking up Siptar terrorist gangs in the sector of the Gredec mountain, retaining a total of 887 individuals who are strongly suspected of participating in the armed attacks against members of the Republic of Serbia MUP and Yugoslav army. All of those taken to the KPD penal and correctional facility in the village of Smrekovnica for further operative processing. Then it records 17.000 to 19.000 inhabitants willingly left the territory of Vucitrn municipality in their own vehicles. The municipal authorities of local self-government registered a total of 716 families and 7.969 members who were put up on their own accord in the villages of Karace, Donja Sudimlja, Smrekovnica, and Kicic. The municipal authorities distributed food, water, and medicine. Just help us with this: So far as you were concerned, were the people detained, if it's the same people identified as the 887 here, terrorist gangs attacking the MUP and the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is of interest to say that all of us who were taken to the prison of Smrekovnica, we were unarmed. We were civilians. The army had left Studime a night earlier to avoid crimes, and none of us was armed and we did not take part. We were not members of the KLA. Had we been members, we wouldn't have joined the convoy. We would have run away, stayed away from it like others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that become Exhibit 41, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 41.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go without food for three days, thereafter receiving some water and bread? Did you all get diarrhea and were you taken out from time to time from the cells to be dealt with by the police?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct to say that no one turned up for three days to see us, and there were people who had many days who hadn't eaten a thing and that was because of their movement around the mountainous area, and we thought they were going to leave us die from hunger. A day before they brought bread to us, they also allowed water to come to the area, and everybody rushed to there, but after drinking that water that they brought to us, we had diarrhea. All of us were suffering from diarrhea. Later, they brought some tanks, tankers with water. Then some policemen turned up to our rooms to bring some ordinary prisoners, and they also delivered some bread to us, and they called names. They threw the bread to us, pieces of bread to us from a distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken out from the cell from time to time by the police? If so, what did the police do to you?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Time after time, policemen would come and ask, "Who is from the village of Bajgora," for example, or from X village. And then they took them away and they mistreated them, and no one dared not to turn up. And then there were cases when they did not identify themselves. And it was not only the prison wardens who were doing it, but among them, I would like you to know there is Sasa Milojevic, from the village of Druar, who before the war worked as an official in the municipality offices of the village, and Vukotic, the terrible Vukotic, who has committed many murders in the town, as well as in the village of Maxhunaj. He worked in the municipality court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the next exhibit, please, SK11. We'll proceed with the photocopy for the time being. Lay the photocopy of the B/C/S on the ELMO. Thank you very much. Having viewed that, if you would hand that to the witness and the English onto the ELMO. Your Honour, I think that the original produced on the last exhibit -- I'm holding the original for the last exhibit, and I think the original handed in as the last exhibit is this one, but we'll sort that out later. That's for the last exhibit, I think. The one that was handed in for the last exhibit is probably this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document, please - have a look - does this document, headed "The Republic of Serbia," dated the 11th of May - yes, it does appear to - does this read as a request of the Kosovska Mitrovica Correctional Institution?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it record: Since we've been dealing with an enormous number of detained people in need of food and supply in the correctional institution in Smrekovnica, ask the headquarters to provide -- and then potato flour, oil, and so on. In view of the transport requirements under war circumstances and lack of vehicles, asking for passenger, car, van, and a water system. And then for food requirements, 15 to 20 head of cattle and three dairy cows, laying hens. Did you, as a matter of fact, in your time in the prison see any meat or have any meat?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never -- we were never given meat. We were given soup, and we were not allowed to even finish it. Because there was a prison warden who was hitting us with a baton, and we were forced to leave it unfinished. Sometimes we took bread with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next document, Exhibit SK12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number for the last one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The original straight to the overhead projector, please. If we can now place an English translation on the overhead projector, hand the original to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document recording that at a meeting on the 11th of May of the Municipal Crisis Staff of Vucitrn, a decision was made that 150 to 200 head of cattle would be fattened and used for the requirements of the Yugoslav army and police, and that a copy of that decision should be delivered to the veterinary service, the farming cooperative, the army, the Ministry of the Interior, and signed again by Slobodan Doknic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There are other cases when things were sent towards Leposaviq for the needs of the army and the police, and they were considered as free cattle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, we see here Doknic making provision, although he was a civilian - or making provision through his Crisis Staff - for both the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On certain occasions the Crisis Staff was called the Staff for Military, Police, and Humanitarian Affairs. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on with your account of what was happening inside the prison, somewhere between the 12th and 14th day of your detention, were you men taken into rooms for -- or were you initially lined up outside a supervisor's office and then taken into different rooms where you were spoken to by men in civilian clothes, or a man in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took us in groups and took us away to the prison's directorate, where there were many rooms, and then separated us, and we were waiting in turn to be questioned. And there were civilian officials there who were asking questions. They told us that -- for example, they told me that, "You have conducted terrorism in Cicavica and that's where you were captured." And I reacted to that and said that, "You captured me -- or you got me in Studime, not in Cicavica, and that I'm an activist of human rights and freedoms, and I went there to check the situation, the humanitarian situation, which was very difficult." And he turned to me and said, "No one is asking you to say that." And we didn't communicate later since that moment. And he was dictating and his secretary was writing, and we were forced to sign that document. And I remember a person, 68 years old - he was ill. He was very ill - in the prison cells, and he did not know how to write. And so they forced him -- they got his finger and he put his finger as a kind of signature or stamp on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these documents that you were compelled to sign, were you given a copy of them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave each and every one of us a copy of these documents, where we were accused of having committed terrorist acts, including that 70-year-old man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: All were civilians. All of us were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the copy that you were given of yours?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd, a day before that, people were taken away and we did not know where they were taken to. On the 23rd they called up our names. A policeman who had thrown across his shoulders a chain of bullets --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must stop you for a minute. It's a very simple question. What happened to the copy of the document that was provided to you? Just tell us in a sentence.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say: As we were coming out of the prison, we saw the same people who were there when we entered. It was Janic and Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's very difficult, Mr. Kadriu, for us to assimilate a huge amount of information which you are trying to give us. Now, I have no doubt you want to tell us, of course, the very important events which happened to you, but in order for us to be able to retain and obtain the important information, you must concentrate on what counsel says. Now, just going back to something, who was it who was asking you questions in the prison? If you don't know his name, just tell us what sort of a person he was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand. The person who was questioning us, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Was he a policeman? Was he from the prison? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know him. I hadn't seen him before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And if I understand you right, he got you to sign a document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And what was on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They gave a copy of that document to us, me included, and we had a copy of the document with ourselves. But then on the 23rd of May, they forced us to hand them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one other thing about this exercise where you signed this document: Did the civilian, the man dressed in civilian clothes in the prison, did he inspect your identification documents, your ID documents?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not mine, but some people were deprived of carrying their identity documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you kept yours at that time?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we kept them until we reached the border with Albania, where they took all of the documents that we were carrying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to come to that in sequence, you see. Following this business of signing the document that you did sign, was there another influx of a number of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were prisoners coming non-stop, and they were coming from the Mitrovica region, and from the 17th of May, there was an extraordinary influx of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were trucks coming all day full of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit SK13, then, next. Your Honour will remember that I earlier said that there were declarations about the problems of all these documents, of some of them, the documents that we are producing that have been produced before they arrive at the witness. They have, of course, been made available to the amici, and indeed to the accused, but if there's anything that arises, it may be the amici will be able to deal with it and we can save burdening the docket with these additional declarations. They're available if wanted. Now, this document, then, if we can have the English version on the overhead projector now, now that the original has been viewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the department of the Interior at Vucitrn on the 16th of May, to the head of the police department and to the duty service shift leader, under the heading "Kosovska Mitrovica," says: "On the 16th of May, 1999, in the course of their work aimed at suppressing the activities of the Siptar terrorist gangs, members of the police force of the Kosovska Mitrovica Secretariat of the Interior detained a total of 830 men of military age who were members of the Siptar national minority. All of them were put up in the penal and correctional facility in Smrekovnica, where operative work will be conducted with them to determine whether they were possibly involved in crimes as members of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army." And does that recorded transfer of, in this case, 830 men match the sort of numbers of people arriving at the prison at the time you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably at the beginning, when we were taken to prison, we were about a thousand in there, but later, when the other influx was taken to the Smrekovnica Prison, we could say there were about 3.000 people, and that was also explained by the enormous amount of food that was required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 44.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of prisoners being taken to the basement? When they were taken there, did you hear sounds coming from the basement?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I was at that part of the prison. Nearby there was a small building with a basement, and several people were taken to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear noises coming from the basement when they had been taken there?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After we had been there for several days, the people there were mistreated. I remember a person who was in there, in the afternoon, who was taken there in the afternoon, and the tortures continued against him. And we were silent in the cell where we were because we could hear the cries coming from him, and we were hearing everything from the window of the cell. I was secretly lurking, staying there, and I saw Sasa Milojevic and the prison warden. And they were pale in the face, and we understood that something had happened to that person, but we were not sure exactly what happened to him. I didn't know the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you on one occasion see a body in a blanket being brought up from those stairs?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following day, in the morning, the police patrol came there and collected those people. The same police car but with some civilians on came out and took out of the basement someone wrapped in a blanket. It was covered in a grey blanket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some days later, were you with other men put in trucks and driven to Mitrovica, the truck first stopping at the technical school. Sorry, the first truck stopping at the technical school with you and some others?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you said at the beginning, I cannot remember exactly the date, but it was between the 18th or the 19th. They sent two trucks. They loaded us -- loaded us on two trucks towards Mitrovica, and they left us at the medical school, the secondary medical school, and there they started mistreating us, and at the same time we were questioned by the prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who mistreated you? What category of person?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we arrived in the secondary medical school, they took us inside the gym of the school, which was close to the main building of the school. We were lined up with our hands behind our heads and kneeling down. There were five -- four or five rows of people like that. And the prison wardens were hitting us on the back and were calling names on us. They were humiliating us. And those people who could not resist the hits and kicks, they fell down. They collapsed. And there were some young people there who were kicking us and hitting us with rods. And then these young men were taken away after they had done this to us. Sometimes they mistreated us, and sometimes there were people who were playing basketball in the gym. And there were people who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bleeding after the mistreatment. And my left leg was numb, and I was dragging it when I was taken to -- when I was being asked to walk away from there. My left leg was numb. I couldn't move it. I was dragging it. And the position we were asked to stay at was also very difficult, with our hands behind our heads, tied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The young people who were beating you, were they of an age to be members of the police or the army or anything of that sort? Did they have any uniform that suggested they were part of an official grouping or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't dare turn our heads to see. But from their voices, from the way they were talking, we could understand that they were adolescents. They were young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've spoken of prison wardens. Is this a separate category of person from the police or not or can't you help us?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prison wardens had distinct uniforms which were different from those of the police, but they cooperated very well with each other. And there were policemen coming to the prison, and they took them away from the prison, mistreated them, manhandled them. And they played music while they mistreated people. Every now and then, they -- they called people from this village and then from another village. In turn they called people from individual villages, and they mistreated them. You had to be very courageous, very brave not to identify yourself as coming from a particular village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while at the school?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened to me that I was called, I was taken away halfway through the period. And I was aching all over. I was covered in sweat. And when I arrived at the investigator's office, I was questioned by two civilians who I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the nature of the things they said to you? Very, very shortly. Just a sentence.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked us -- of course they knew that I was an activist of the Council of Human Rights and Freedoms. They had that information. And they asked me whether any of my relatives was a member of the KLA, and they were putting provoking questions to me about the problems over the years as if -- they were asking me, "Why did you do this?" and, "Why did you do that?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's enough for the time being. Were you physically maltreated in the course of interrogation or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only me. All of us were maltreated. Very much so, I would say. Sometimes they beat us with sticks, batons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you returned to the prison from the school?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At about 5.00, they returned us to the prison. First it was our truck that returned and then the others followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it at about this time that you returned, because you were forced to, the documents you had earlier signed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to hand over the documents on the day we were released from prison, which was 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, where were you taken and how?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all this that we went through in the prison of Smrekovnica, they loaded us on some buses. I'm not sure of the number. We had to wait for some time. Then they drove us to some unknown direction but passing through Vushtrri. We didn't know where they were taking us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of this journey, were others allowed onto the bus to do things to you?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all the time with our hands tied behind our back. When we arrived in Shtime, in the town of Shtime, which is situated in the vicinity of Ferizaj along the way from Pristina to Prizren, the buses stopped. There were also policemen in the buses who were taking away the last money we had on us. And they started to speak to some Gypsies who were close by and were watching. Then they threw open the doors of the buses and those Gypsies entered the buses and started to beat us up. I think the buses that were before us suffered worst. We waited there until some trucks arrived of a dark green colour. There were some soldiers with bandanas around their heads. Some were -- had long hair. They had -- they had worn different uniforms. I can't say they had the same uniform. Then they were -- they stayed before our bus, so they were situated in between the buses. We waited there for an hour. Then we left for Suhareke and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you end up eventually, taking this story comparatively shortly?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Zhur village, the graveyard of Zhur village. The cemetery was on -- on a forest. We saw a large number of police forces who had surrounded the place. I don't remember if there were also army troops. I'm not sure about that. They ordered us to get off the buses, and they kept beating us with their arms, bats, and kicking us and beating us with anything they could lay hands on. They forced us to line up. I am speaking about my bus, the bus I was in, I mean. Then they told us, "Go that way and never look back, and you must run." And they kept beating and kicking us all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move as fast as you were able?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of us started to run. Professor -- Professor Bajram Mulaku and myself, we could not run. We ran for a little while, but as I said, my leg was hurting me. I couldn't run. And our hands were tied behind our heads. And in this state we went up to the border point separating Albania from Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the border, what happened so far as your documents were concerned?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the border, we had to wait in a column, because before us there were people who got off the other buses. There we -- there were about seven or eight policemen there and were waiting for us. They told us to show everything we had in our pockets, all the documents, and to keep them in our hands. And they warned us that if they would check us and find some documents in the pocket, "You will see what will happen to you." And some of us were very upset because their IDs, their passports, were taken away in the Smrekovnica prison. And they turned to one of the policemen and said to him that, "We don't have our IDs because they were taken away in the prison." They said, "Come here, each and every one of you. Even the driving licence, all the documents you have on you, you should keep them in your hand and keep walking in a line." We kept walking in a line in front of them, and then we went on to Albania after we handed over to these policemen every document we had on us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you went to Albania, was anything said to you by the Serbs at the border?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were there, those guards, when we were waiting to go to the border, one of them came and cursed us and said, "You want to be with Albania," while he was speaking ill of our mothers, saying words about our mothers. He said, "Go to Albania, and you'll never return." We felt in a very bad situation, because we felt this was the last time for us to see Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay in Albania in various refugee camps until the 19th of June of 1999, when you returned to Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed in a camp funded by the Spanish government in the vicinity of Dures, put up for the refugees coming from Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On return, did you become deputy mayor, or deputy president as we referred to it yesterday, of the municipality, and did you also become president of the War Crime Commission for Vushtrri in which capacity you have been collecting, as is clear, documents recording things that happened in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that capacity, may we look at a few more exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that would be a convenient moment. We'll have a short break. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few documents. SK14 next, please. It can go straight to the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you've told us already about the connection of the army and the police, and you've told us about the role of the Crisis Staff, and we're looking at these documents just with a few points of an associated kind. This first document is dated the 26th of May of 1999. So just about the time you were leaving for Albania. And from the Vucitrn Municipal Administration here to the "Municipal Council of the Municipality, Displaced Persons, Municipal Headquarters," and it reads as follows: "On the basis of the felt need, we ask you to provide the following items to meet the requirements of the conscripts of the 54 /VTOd, Territorial Defence Platoon in Vucitrn," and it sets out various items. The -- the Territorial Defence Platoon of the Territorial Defence, did you see anything of them in the course of these events?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document we have here shows that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I must ask you, please, to listen to the question. Mr. Nice, would you repeat the question. Don't bother about the document for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything of the Territorial Defence in the course of the events you've described?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen many civilian persons. I mean, many members who used to be working in various civilian offices, were recruited in these Territorial Defence platoons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second question: This document, what does it show us, from your knowledge, of how the Territorial Defence was obtaining its equipment?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence were obtaining their equipment through the Crisis Management Staff, for anything they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The same. So that's the same staff as we've been looking at earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next Exhibit, please, SK15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Next exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can now look at the English version on the overhead projector. This is a document, I think, that's a note signed by the same Slobodan Doknic, and the note records that the Vucitrn Municipality Crisis Staff confirms the purchase of ten combat jackets for the Yugoslav army. The note is issued for tax exemption and so on. So here we have a document from Doknic providing or arranging for the provision of the material for the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that fit with your understanding of what the Crisis Staff was doing?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Crisis Staff coordinated its work very well with the military authorities. This certificate proves this to the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document -- I'm sorry. Exhibit --?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 46. Next document, SK17 -- I'm sorry, 16. Exhibit SK16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While you're waiting, the 18.200 dinars would be how much in US dollars, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I actually can't tell you. I don't know whether the witness can give us the approximate dinar exchange rate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or what the combat jacket is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The combat jacket. It's 1.800 dinars per combat jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much would that translate into dollars as at 1999?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thousand, eight hundred dinars would be equivalent to - an approximate figure - of about 6.000 Deutschmark. That was the rate of dinar to the Deutschmark then, around this figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If right, a rather expensive jacket. Can we look at the next document, then, SK16. If the original now can go to the witness, having been displayed on the overhead projector. The English version tells us that this is a document recording a meeting on the 28th of May -- a meeting of the coordination of Civil, Army, Police, and Humanitarian Affairs headquarter, a decision about the establishment of a commission for abandoned vehicles. The composition of the commission is identified, and its duty is identified as gathering abandoned vehicles, and so on. There is also, I think -- let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, this is the same body, is it, Mr. Kadriu, that we've been concerned with, however it's headed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The name is different. It's the same signature, the same name of the person who has signed it, but only the heading is different. The staff for civilian, military, police, and humanitarian coordination of the Vushtrri municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need from that. And then I think the document of this kind --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. SK17. This document, then - English version now, please, to the overhead projector - 6th of June, from the Vucitrn municipality coordination headquarters, signed by Slobodan Doknic again, a request for release from conscription, asks that the above-named war unit, which is set out above, release conscript Petar Toplicevic from conscription since he is --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- indispensable to the Vucitrn Prevos [phoen] company due to public transport requirements under war circumstances. So that here we have the same president of the Crisis Staff, or otherwise described, being required for the transportation of public transport requirements under war circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Well, that's all I want from that type of document, and I've got a few more topics, but very few, to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 48.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, in the course of your function for the war crimes commission, you prepared or had prepared reports, I think.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to some extent. This is only the tip of the iceberg of the entire campaign of violence and terror that was perpetrated. We tried to do our utmost, but we didn't have the necessary conditions to work properly. This is very little by comparison to the large-scale violence and terror.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've managed to bring some reports with you. We've looked at the one on the convoy and we may look at a little bit of video if we have time in due course, but can we go now to the - I'm not sure of the pronunciation - Gerxhaliu family massacre, please. First of all, what's the correct pronunciation of the family's name?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gerxhaliu. Thank you. And have you brought with you a report that was prepared in respect of what happened to that family on the 31st of May, when, of course, you were already in Albania yourself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Albania myself, but the documents about this massacre we prepared after my return from Albania, on the basis of photos and evidence. It was a very tragic event that occurred on the morning of 31st of May. The house of Selatin Gerxhaliu was surrounded by Serb forces stationed in Rashica neighbourhood. After they surrounded the house, all the family members were put in a room. Selatin and two others were taken to another place. The other members, including women and children, were all executed in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I hand, then, in the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, again an evidential point arises about the status of this evidence. It's quite clearly based entirely on information provided for this witness, it hasn't been served as an expert's report on any of the other parties in this case, it's completely without notice. It's coming through the witness as he's giving evidence, and one really wonders what the usefulness of this evidence is to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this case there are photographs, as well as other documents that were prepared contemporaneously, and I think they will be of assistance, because the photographs themselves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we find out what role the witness played in the preparation of this report? He used the word "we." He uses it very often, and it's not at all clear what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've heard His Honour's question. What part did your commission play, what part did you play personally, in the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were a commission. Our role was to collect information about the number of people killed, massacred, and disappeared. My role was that of a coordinator of its work. We collected all -- that is, the commission collected all the documents related to different places and persons. It is true, as I said, that we didn't succeed in collecting all the material that there is on such cases, but the most conspicuous ones are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have the point. He was the coordinator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall admit this report. The witness was close enough to it and played an important enough role as coordinator to allow him to produce it. It is the practice in the Tribunal to receive reports of this sort. It will be for the Tribunal to assess what weight to place upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I distribute the original to the witness. Then there are colour copies - one, two, three, four, five, six - and two in black and white, and there are then translations of the legends associated with the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, while we are waiting again, are these Gerxhaliu family members, 11 of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- included in the victims of murder cases? We have Schedule H in the indictment. Could you check it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's page 53 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I should have checked that in advance. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are a lot of Gerxhalius in the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I think we'll have an answer either from myself or from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were over 33 people who were executed that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the indictment, it said 104 persons were killed at the murder site, and that seems to me that it means the convoy massacre of the Gerxhaliu family. So could you clarify later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I may have to clarify a little later. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And the date of the murder was written as May 2nd, not 31st.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On both of those points, can you help, us, please, about the date of this massacre, the Gerxhaliu family massacre.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The people executed from Gerxhaliu family comprise over 30 persons. They were executed on the 31st of May, but of the overall number of people killed on the 2nd of May, this is not -- the number 104 is not included. One hundred nine were executed, but 104 have the graves in this mass cemetery that the ICTY has exhumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can look at this document, and showing the photographs as necessary on the ELMO and working through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there a spare copy for the usher to lay on the ELMO? And if the witness can keep the original with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first page is a plan which shows the house, the heading being that the -- it's called "Selatin Family." Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the scheme of the house of Selatin Gerxhaliu. In the legend it says -- number 1, it says it shows the door of courtyard, because we have yards, courtyards in our homes. Number 2 shows the door of the house which leads to a corridor. Then number 3, the door of the corridor where the massacre was perpetrated of all the members of the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we have --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 4 shows the beds on which the family members were sleeping. It was still early morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we then go to --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can go to the photographs now, having understood that. The first photograph simply shows some of the family I think some years before, but before death, before they obviously -- while they were alive. If we then go to F1, which is said to be the photograph of -- perhaps you'll pronounce the name for me properly.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fegjrije Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: F2, show us, please.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corridor where they were killed, the members of the Gerxhaliu family were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second photograph shows, I think, the beds in the room where several people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The usher has got the wrong one on the projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one, F1.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Fegjria Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And underneath that, F2.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows from another angle the place where several members of the Gerxhaliu family were executed, the state in which they were found after they were executed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the page to F3.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: F3 shows the listless body of Sofije Gerxhaliu, who was at this posture where she was after the execution.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shows the place where Selatin and Shaban Gerxhaliu were massacred outside the house. They were taken out of the house, taken to another place where they were executed and massacred. You can see on their forehead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read out, because it's been omitted from the key, can you read out what is said under F5, please.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: F5 shows the bed on which a young girl, Mybera Gerxhaliu, was killed. You see she was trying to reach her mother when she heard the shots, automatic shots. She has tried to reach to her mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can see the rest of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the remaining photographs are self-explanatory, perhaps, with the guide to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one point as a matter of detail. If we could turn over to the last page, please, and focus not on the particular distressing photograph on the left but on the grave on the right. Just as a matter of detail, because we may come upon this later. Not that one. The photograph on the right, please, usher. The grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a minute. Can you go, please, to the -- that's right. The photograph on the right. Yes. Leave it like that. That's fine. Can the -- no, not that one. The one at the top right-hand corner, please. All right. We can see a little bit of it. I don't want to look at the body. I want to look at the grave on the right. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we see there an open grave, and we see some boards, slats of wood, to the right, cut to perhaps a uniform length. Can you just explain -- it may turn up later in other witnesses. Can you explain, please, how these boards are used for the process of burying bodies in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The police executed them and left. Then this grave shows that because of the shortage of time, people were scared that something else might happen to them. They dug up this grave quickly, and the planks of wood usually are used before throwing the earth over the dead body. Instead of the coffin, that is, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I right, and correct me if I'm wrong, the board's lowered over the body but at an angle, and the intention is to keep the earth off the body.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We may see that repeated elsewhere. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Your Honour, if we look at the -- if Your Honour would be good enough to look at the summary. Although that particular event happens to have been documented here, the witness is also able to tell us about a great many other killings of which the most important ones have been highlighted in the summary. The others come without documentary support so that they would be effectively the same but it would simply be coming from his mouth. And I would ask leave to make very brief reference to each of them, and I will ensure that the witness is brief in dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would single out here on the 2nd of May, when we were the agriculture cooperative --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was going to single it out, actually. So if you wouldn't mind very much just listening to what I'm going to ask you. I'm going to ask you questions that will be susceptible to very short answers, and I want you to tell the Judges about that. On the 22nd of May, was there an event concerning people who had returned to their homes in Vushtrri and were walking towards the cemetery? Simply yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was an event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the inquiries that your commission made, were they stopped by a house owned by Sezaj Pasome, by Serbs in green camouflage uniforms? Yes or no will do.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage, with masks --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and accompanied by motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the, I think, 74 people concerned on that incident, how many have never been accounted for?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seventy-four people on the 22nd of May are still unaccounted for. And on behalf of their families, I would ask this Court to do something to know -- to find out about the destiny of these people. But number -- the overall number of those who are considered disappeared are 109.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'll -- but as to these 74, the material you collected suggested that shots were heard and that blood was found in the area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the body of a man called Shefki Dallku found in the house of Dr. Ramadan Xhoni?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Not far from the house of Sezaj Pasome, 50 metres away. His body was exhumed from the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then over the page. Reznik, on the 6th of April, according to your inquiries --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 6th of April, in the afternoon, were members of the Ujkani family --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ujkani family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were involved?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly nine, nine members of the Ujkani family were executed. Among the nine, as far as I remember, three were women. There was a couple, a married couple, and some others. They were brothers of the same family, Ujkani family. Some of the bodies were even burned, because the houses were torched and the bodies were inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your inquiries, were gunshots heard there as well?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. According to the eyewitnesses who made statements on this, on this case, on this occasion there were gunshots and then houses torched, and there were people inside, those who were executed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally on this topic, and subject to the tape of the convoy, on the 24th of May of 1999, near Studime e Eperme, according to information were there women who were attacked?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were coming to collect food for their children and to take food to the Studime e Eperme village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- I think it was a local KLA commander who collected the bodies. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because no one dared to come and collect the bodies. That's why soldiers from the KLA went there to collect the bodies, the lifeless bodies of the women, because the Serb forces were not far from the scene of the crime. Probably 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many dead women involved?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were eight, eight women, as far as I remember. They were not all women. Some of them were girls, little girls. They were raped, mutilated, completely mutilated, and they were found -- the bodies were found in a terrible state. And the surviving members of their family are still suffering from shock, from the trauma they suffered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "mutilated," just give us a couple of examples of what was done to them.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the testimony of family members, of the surviving family members, the girls and women had bruised the parts of their bodies, and they were stained with blood. Some of them did not have fingers, things were cut off, and some bodies lacked certain limbs. Initially they were -- they were raped - and I'm sorry to say this in public - and they were shot afterwards in the most savage, inhuman way. The bodies were found in the village of Studime e Poshtme, as they were crossing the river, because the riverbed was the area which gave you the opportunity to -- to walk along and move around unnoticed. But they were ambushed and killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I return the Chamber very briefly to page 7 of the summary in case these details need cross-referencing later. It's unlikely but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, Mr. Kadriu, to take your memory back to the September offensive and just to say yes or no to these questions: In the September offensive, was there the killing of a 50-year-old man in the village called Beciq? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the September offensive, many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include one man in Beciq whose name you've provided?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And two men in Balinca?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw these men, and I think you estimate their ages as what?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hyseni was about 60 years old, and I saw his body, his mutilated body, lifeless body. They were buried on the same day when the funeral took place in Oshlan, because Balinca is not far from Oshlan. They're very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think I still have to deal with in Smrekovnica there was a man I think you saw there killed in his yard.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was before the 22nd of September. One was killed as he came out to the courtyard of his house. Initially he was wounded. And then from a close distance, he was shot behind his ear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And his brains were scattered around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another one was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to page 16 of the summary. Can you help us with the total figures of victims for your municipality as revealed in the exercises you engaged in? How many people killed in 1999? Forget 1998. In 1999, how many civilians killed by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the statistics, which are also in possession of the Pristina Council for Human Rights and Freedoms in Pristina, there are 594 civilians killed by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of those under the age of 18 at the time of death?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly those figures. I couldn't say that. I have had to remember very many figures and dates. I'm sorry, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the number injured by -- injured in some significant way by Serb forces? And if not, just say so.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than 300 wounded, injured civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many civilians still missing, not accounted for?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are 109 civilians missing, and there are 74 only from a date in May. And I have pictures of each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of these events, what number of children have been identified as having one or both of their parents killed in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I can't remember the figures. If you allow me, I do have the exact statistics, but I can't remember them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The total number of houses burnt? Do you know roughly or precisely what that was?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more than 8.000 houses were shelled, were demolished, were torched. And they have been classified into three categories; one, two, three. More than 4.000 houses belong to a fifth category, to a fifth group, which is that of houses which need to be rebuilt from scratch, more than 4.000 houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many mosques destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, because there were also many cattle, sheep, and other livestock which was destroyed then, but I wouldn't like to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the tape, the compilation tape of the convoy, which we passed over comparatively briefly, would take 5 minutes and 55 seconds to play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have an index of the passages that are being played, and I'll distribute those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the index, and we'll play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In answer to His Honour's question, none of the names that we've given are actually scheduled in the indictment. If the tape could be played, and if I'll be permitted to read the legend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, we see villagers gathering in a field and a tractor coming down a hill. This is the second excerpt, and it shows clearly soldiers talking to the villagers. There's a general view of villagers and displaced persons in a field, including, I think you may already have seen, a picture of a very young child. Now you'll see some evidence of destruction following an attack. A destroyed tractor is immediately apparent, and smoking houses in the background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can the witness tell us where the village is that we are looking at from this position?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Houses destroyed after the attack, the convoy, and a man collecting timber for the purpose of the burial that I dealt with in the still photograph, not the particular funeral, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The boards are used for the burial process, for the burial of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now looking at some bodies that were killed in the attack on the convoy. Burial of some of the victims. There's a woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the only question you didn't answer, probably because you didn't understand I was asking you a question, Mr. Kadriu: Where we were looking at houses that were burning, we were looking over a valley or towards the other side of a valley, it would appear, can you tell us which that village was we were looking at, or you are unable to say?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were looking at the Studime e Eperme village, and also part of the road between the two villages, Studime e Eperme and Studime e Poshtme. And the burial took place not far from Studime e Eperme, where the bodies -- close to the site where the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be sensible to give that compilation an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 13/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Before we break, was there something you wanted to raise about Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About witness order, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if we can deal with it just in private session. I don't know if the Chamber is going to do that. It involves one protected witness. If we can just go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
